newsitem.title: UK: ATHLETICS-KOMEN AIMS TO ADD A GOLD MEDAL TO HIS COFFERS..
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-KOMEN AIMS TO ADD A GOLD MEDAL TO HIS COFFERS..

text.p: Daniel Komen, current world record holder over 3,000 metres and two miles, remains a king without a crown.
The 21-year-old Kenyan missed out on the 1995 world championships and the 1996 Olympics because of niggling injuries.
This year he intends to make amends and win a gold medal at the Athens world championships.
"My eyes are all the time on Athens," Komen said in an interview.
"Everyone knows I can run fast but now I say to myself that maybe I need to be a world champion for people to think of me as a great runner. I'm praying day and night for this to happen."
Komen has already indicated that it will take a special talent to beat him in Athens, if he remains injury free.
He opened his 1997 outdoor campaign by clocking 13 minutes 3.51 seconds over 5,000 metres at the Osaka grand prix on May 10. No one has ever run faster outdoors so early in the year.

His immediate racing plans, after concluding a current training stint in Switzerland, are a 5,000 metres at the Golden Gala meeting in Rome on June 5 and 3,000 metres three days later in Moscow before returning to Kenya to prepare for the national trials at the end of June.
Although the race in Rome has been billed as an attempt on Ethiopian Haile Gebrselassie's world best of 12:44.39, Komen has discounted the possibility.
"I do not think that is possible at this stage in the season. It's too early but I will still be looking for fast times."
Once the world championships are behind him, though, he intends to show the world that there are no limits to his ability.
"I can run much faster over 5,000 metres, especially over the last two laps. This should mean a world record."
One race that does not feature on his schedule is the two mile race at the Hengelo meeting on May 31 where Algeria's Noureddine Morceli will meet Gebrselassie.
Both runners will be aiming to improve on Komen's present world best of eight minutes 3.54 seconds.
One million dollars is on offer if the winner stops the clock in less than eight minutes.
Komen is aggrieved that he has not been allowed on the start line.
"I was hoping to be in that race. I'd like to take on both runners but I can understand why adidas do not want me in the race," he said.
The sportswear company are not only the Hengelo race sponsors but also the individual sponsors of both Morceli and Gebrselassie while Komen is sponsored by arch-rival Nike.
"I know the two miles is not a distance that is often run but I am preparing to break that world record as well," added Komen.

"If Morceli or Gebrselassie run faster than eight minutes in Hengelo then I will run faster still and if they do not then I will be the first man under eight minutes when I race over two miles later this summer."
Komen knows that he has nothing to prove as far as fast times are concerned.
But how is he going to avoid the fate of Australian Ron Clarke or American Jim Ryun who both ran many world best times but never won a major title?
"I've spent many hours watching videos of other runners. I have been learning the techniques of winning races for three years since I was a world junior champion," he said.
"Before I was running races without planning. Now I am almost ready for anything Gebrselassie might do if I face him in Athens. Even a runner as good as him is not perfect!"
